This 6-year-old male with sickle cell disease and chronic granulomatous disease, recently diagnosed with ataxia-telangiectasia by Pediatric Neurology in January, presents with fever, productive cough, and shortness of breath that began 2 days ago.
His parents say he has also been more tired than usual, refusing to play, and has had decreased appetite.
The cough produces yellow sputum, and he has complained of mild right-sided chest pain when breathing deeply.

The boy was diagnosed at age 3 with an inherited immunodeficiency after a history of recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, including several hospitalizations for pneumonia and two episodes of suppurative cervical lymphadenitis.
His past positive cultures have grown Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia marcescens , and Burkholderia cepacia .
At the time of his diagnosis, he underwent special blood testing that demonstrated absent oxidative burst in neutrophils.
He has never had major viral illnesses outside of typical colds, and his vaccinations are up to date.
He has also had a cutaneous abscess on his thigh that required incision and drainage.
His medical regimen includes daily trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and itraconazole prophylaxis, as well as subcutaneous interferon-gamma injections three times a week.
His parents admit they recently ran out of his prophylactic medications due to a delay in prescription refills.
Home Medications:
- Penicillin V potassium 125 mg orally twice daily for sickle cell prophylaxis
- Interferon gamma-1b 50 mcg/m2 subcutaneous injection three times weekly for CGD immunomodulation
No known drug allergies
Family history is notable for a maternal uncle who had recurrent bacterial infections in childhood and died in his teens of pneumonia.
The patient’s younger sister is healthy.
He lives with his parents and sister in a suburban home and attends school regularly, although he has missed many days this year due to illness.
There is no tobacco exposure in the household.
On examination, his temperature is 38.9°C (102.0°F), pulse 115/min, blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg, respiratory rate 26/min, and oxygen saturation 91% on room air.
The boy appears tired but is alert and interactive.
Pulmonary auscultation reveals diffuse crackles and coarse breath sounds over the right lower lung field with mild subcostal retractions.
The remainder of the exam is normal except for a well-healed scar on the right thigh from prior surgery.
Laboratory evaluation shows leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance.
Blood cultures grow a gram-negative rod that is oxidase positive, catalase positive, and motile, with intrinsic resistance to multiple antibiotics.
Chest x-ray demonstrates right lower lobe consolidation with mild air bronchograms.
